title: Why big female pythons may matter most in Florida
summary:
The Burmese python is a huge snake that does not belong in Florida. It is an invasive species, which means it came from another place and causes problems for local wildlife. Florida has an estimated 100,000-300,000 of these predators. It is legal to hunt them all year, and the state holds an annual 10-day competition to see who can catch the most.

A new study in the journal Ecological Applications says that catching any python may not be the best plan. Ecologist Alex Romer of the University of Florida said, "Our previous work treated all Burmese pythons as contributing equally to the population." But removing the biggest female they have ever caught is very different from removing a tiny snake that might not survive next year.

The team studied data from the South Florida Water Management District's Python Elimination Program. They created a scoring system called the Weighted Removal Index. A snake earns points based on its age, its sex and the time of year. Young snakes score lower because many do not live long enough to breed. Researchers suggest focusing on mature female pythons. An adult female regularly lays around 70 eggs at a time. Romer said "a big female might be worth 100 arbitrary ecological points, while a little snake might be worth five."

The team also says organizers may want to move the hunting contest, now held in the summer, to winter. In months like January or February, fewer pythons are removed, but their scores are much higher because most of them are adults.
why_it_matters: Invasive species can crowd out local wildlife. Smart plans that target the animals that matter most may help people use their time and effort better.
